newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya's Odinga quits party, parliament.
newsitem.headline: Kenya's Odinga quits party, parliament.

text.p: Leading Kenyan politician Raila Odinga on Tuesday resigned from the main opposition FORD-Kenya party and as member of parliament to form a new party, further splintering the opposition.
Political analysts in Nairobi said the latest split in Kenya's opposition ranks had come as good news to President Daniel arap Moi, who will be seeking re-election in 1997.
Opposition wrangles were largely responsible for Moi's return to power in landmark 1992 pluralist presidential polls -- the first in nearly 30 years.

Odinga, a 51-year-old charismatic and combative politician, told a news conference he was forming the National Development Party of Kenya (NDPK) to contest parliamentary and presidential elections due some time in 1997.
"I have resigned from FORD-Kenya party and have notified the parliament speaker of my standing down as a member of parliament," Odinga said.
Odinga said leadership wrangles in FORD-Kenya, this east African country's biggest opposition party, had forced him to quit and form a new party he says will exercise internal democracy.
"It has reached a point where FORD-Kenya could not be salvaged and continued wrangling in the party means that members cannot exercise their right of choice of leaders," Odinga added.
Raila Odinga is the son of the late black African nationalist and Kenya's first vice-president at independence from Britain in 1963, Jaramogi Oginga Odinga.
The elder Odinga was later to become the doyen of Kenya's opposition politics and successfully campaigned for the reintroduction of pluralist politics in Kenya in December 1991. He died in 1994.
The move by the younger Odinga, who commands a large following amongst Kenya's third biggest tribe, the Luos, followed two years of leadership wrangling in the FORD-Kenya party.

Odinga, who until Kenya's switch to pluralist politics was the country's best-known political prisoner, had unsuccessfully tried to oust his father's successor Michael Kijana Wamalwa as chairman of the country's biggest opposition party.
The two men headed separate FORD-Kenya factions and Wamalwa announced over a week ago that he had expelled Odinga from FORD-Kenya. At the time Odinga rejected the move as "rubbish".
FORD-Kenya party was founded in 1992. It was a splinter from the FORD (Forum for the Restoration of Democracy) party led by the elder Odinga.
The party split into two after leadership differences between the elder Odinga and another opposition leader Kenneth Matiba.
